strengths: Addresses a relevant limitation of offline sequence-based RL: retaining information beyond a transformer's context window while using fixed-length segment computation.

Provides concrete evidence of useful memory: RATE achieves 100% T-Maze success through three segments, and RATE-7 achieves 99.3% at five segments. Atari results, particularly Qbert, also substantially improve over the reported DT baseline.

Evaluation spans two memory tasks, four Atari games, and nine MuJoCo settings. Curriculum, memory perturbation, segment-count, and memory-size ablations provide useful supporting evidence; hyperparameters and an implementation link are included.
weaknesses: Novelty and baseline coverage are insufficiently established. RATE principally combines existing RMT memory tokens, Transformer-XL recurrence, and DT tokenization. The memory-critical tasks lack matched recurrent-policy and Transformer-XL-only baselines. Moreover, RATE without memory tokens already scores 12,300 on Qbert versus 13,518 for RATE and 2,215.8 for DT, so most of this headline improvement does not establish the contribution of the added tokens.

Comparisons confound architecture with training and inference choices. RATE samples episode prefixes containing the initial cue, whereas DT samples random subsequences. For MuJoCo, RATE additionally resets the target return at segment boundaries while comparing against published baseline scores. Matched sampling and return-conditioning controls are needed to attribute improvements to memory.

The central training procedure is technically ambiguous. Section 3 says the recurrent memory is detached, but immediately states that gradients flow through it into the preceding segment. Explicit recurrence equations or pseudocode must clarify stop-gradient locations, cross-segment backpropagation, and optimizer updates; these choices affect both learnability and computational requirements.

The VizDoom memory-isolation claim needs clarification. Rewards are supposedly withheld because they reveal the target color, yet consecutive return-to-go inputs updated using observed rewards reveal those rewards through their difference. This potentially permits recovering the target color after item collection. Appendix B explores constant returns, but does not repeat the main DT comparison under that control.

The claimed significant VizDoom improvement is not established by the reported uncertainty: reward is 16.46 ± 6.90 for RATE versus 6.08 ± 1.62 for DT90, with values labeled as standard errors. The manuscript provides no statistical analysis supporting this claim, and the default three training seeds are inadequate for resolving such high variability.

Evidence for general long-term memory remains narrow. Both memory benchmarks center on an initial binary cue, and ordinary RATE-7 success drops to 66.1% at twelve T-Maze segments. The reported 100K retention requires freezing the first segment's memory, rather than using the normal recurrent update. Richer memory tasks and measured runtime/GPU-memory comparisons are needed to substantiate broader capacity and efficiency claims.
